newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: Intervention in NZ dollar won't work, say analysts.
newsitem.headline: Intervention in NZ dollar won't work, say analysts.

text.p: New Zealand foreign exchange analysts on Monday dismissed as counter-productive apparent hints by Labour Party finance spokesman Michael Cullen that the central bank should directly intervene in the market.

Cullen, who is Labour's candidate for finance minister if it clinches a coalition with the New Zealand First party, caused a mild stir in financial markets last week when he sent a coded message about intervention.
New Zealand First is expected to decide on Tuesday whether it will support Labour or the conservative National Party.
In his speech, Cullen said there were various "highly orthodox and commonly practised ways" of addressing the exchange rate, which he has consistently described as overvalued.
He declined to go into detail, but said calls for dropping interest rates missed the point and the exchange rate itself was the primary problem.
Foreign exchange experts all took Cullen to mean that the Reserve Bank should intervene directly to bring the dollar down, something never done since the kiwi was floated in March 1985.
The kiwi, which recently touched 8-1/2 year highs, is one of the freest floating currencies in the world but RBNZ Governor Don Brash reserves the right to intervene.
Brash last week told Reuters he did not wish to air his views on intervention. In the past he has pointed to the failure of intervention by other countries, notably Britain in 1992.

"It doesn't work very well and can be counter-productive under certain circumstances. The general view on intervention is that it is not particularly effective," said Bankers Trust economist David Plank.

"The very short term impact (of RBNZ selling) might be for the currency to dip, but the general experience around the world is (intervention is) very ineffective but good at wasting taxpayers' money."

Cullen has argued that part of the reason for the kiwi's steep climb -- up 25 percent on a Trade-Weighted Index basis in three years -- is that investing in the New Zealand dollar is a one-way bet, and he wants to dispel that notion.
Brash caused a stir in the currency market last week when he said that the New Zealand dollar appeared to be near the top of its cycle. Plank believes the currency is 10-15 percent overvalued.
But not everyone agrees.
National Bank chief foreign exchange dealer Stu Nattrass said the exchange rate had only recovered to the level it was at in 1988, after which the country went into deep recession.
He said inflation expectations are the seat of the problem and the reason why wholesale interest rates are at 8.5 percent while inflation is expected to be at one percent in 1997.
"Interest rates are far more relevant than exchange rates. I'm surprised people are focusing on the exchange rate and not interest rates as being way out of line," Nattrass said.
A dealer who did not wish to be named said that if the RBNZ directly sells New Zealand dollars it will simply provide cheap rates for investors to buy the currency.
"You would quickly find a level of willing buyers," he said.
One bank's chief bond dealer said any intervention would indicate the RB's autonomy had been undermined.

"It would not be the amount the bank sold, just that they are sellers. I would see that as being bearish, showing political influence coming back into the Reserve Bank and therefore they are losing their independence," he said.

Under the Reserve Bank Act, the finance minister can request an intervention but the governor is as liberty to ignore it if such a move would threaten the bank's goal of achieving price stability. The government can demand action but needs to get an Order in Council, a move requiring cabinet approval and signature by the governor-general.
Even exporters doubt intervention would work.

Malcolm Bailey, president of lobby group Federated Farmers and spokesman for an exporters' crisis summit on the exchange rate last week, said: "I don't think selling New Zealand dollars will be the answer."
He said exporters are not looking for quick fix solutions, although he agreed intervention could "burst the bubble of over-enthusiasm about investing in New Zealand".
"If you have the government behind the Reserve Bank pulling the levers, then you undermine confidence in the Reserve Bank Act," he said. -- Wellington newsroom 64 4 4734 746
